title: Divisibility Rules
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Mental Shortcuts for Exact Division Testing

introduction.overview: Divisibility rules are instant mental tests that confirm whether one integer exactly divides another — without performing long division. Knowing the rules for 2 to 13 removes a great deal of calculation when filtering options in aptitude questions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Divisibility rules underpin HCF, LCM, simplification, and factor analysis. All major campus placement tests (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant) include 2–4 divisibility-based questions either directly or as sub-steps of larger problems.
introduction.realWorldContext: Every programming language uses modulus (%) to check divisibility. Div-by-2 checks odd/even data routing. Div-by-7 is used in calendar algorithms. Div-by-360 or 365 determines angular and calendar cycles. These rules have direct engineering applications.

learningObjectives: Understand and apply core principles of Divisibility Rules

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Know the tables up to 12 and the meaning of "divisible by" and "remainder".

coreDefinitions: Divisibility: A is divisible by B if A ÷ B gives remainder 0. Written B | A.
Factor/Divisor: B is a factor of A if B | A. Example: 6 is a factor of 42.
Multiple: A is a multiple of B if B | A. Example: 42 is a multiple of 6.
Remainder: A = B×Q + R where 0 ≤ R < B. Divisibility holds when R = 0.
Co-prime Component Rule: If gcd(a,b)=1 and N is divisible by both a and b, then N is divisible by a×b.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Divisibility rules derive from modular arithmetic. Since 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), each digit in any base-10 number contributes its face value to the number's residue mod 9 — giving the digit-sum rule. Since 10 ≡ 0 (mod 5), only the units digit determines divisibility by 5. Each rule has a mathematical reason, not just a pattern to memorize.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Imagine divisibility as 'equal sharing'. Can 144 students be arranged in exactly 9 equal rows? Compute 1+4+4 = 9 → divisible by 9 → yes, 16 per row. This digit-sum shortcut replaces 144 ÷ 9 entirely and takes under 3 seconds.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Divisibility by 2
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Number is even if and only if its last digit is even.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Divisibility by 3
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Sum all digits; divisible by 3 iff sum is.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Divisibility by 4
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Last two digits form a number divisible by 4
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Hundreds and higher place values are always divisible by 4.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Divisibility by 9
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Same as rule for 3 but digit sum must be divisible by 9.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Divisibility by 11
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: (Sum of odd-position digits) − (Sum of even-position digits) ≡ 0 (mod 11)
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Alternating digit sum from rightmost position.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: 29,678: odd-pos from right=8+6+2=16, even-pos=7+9=16. 16-16=0 → divisible by 11.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Total Number of Factors
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Counts all positive divisors of N including 1 and N.

mainNarrative: The rule for 2 is trivially explained: in base 10, every place value above the units (10, 100, 1000, …) is a multiple of 2. So only the units digit contributes to the number's odd/even status. The same logic — powers of 10 divisible by 4 beyond the tens place — explains why only the last two digits determine divisibility by 4, and the last three digits for divisibility by 8.

The digit-sum rules for 3 and 9 arise because 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9). This means 10^k ≡ 1 for every positive k in both mod 3 and mod 9. Therefore any number N = d_n×10^n + … + d_1×10 + d_0 has the same remainder as d_n + … + d_1 + d_0 when divided by 3 or 9. This is why digit sums work perfectly for these divisors.

For divisibility by 7, the standard shortcut is: double the units digit, subtract from the number formed by the remaining digits, and repeat until you reach a small number. If that number is 0 or divisible by 7, the original is too. Example: Is 826 divisible by 7? Double 6 = 12. 82 - 12 = 70. 70 ÷ 7 = 10 → yes. (826 = 7×118 ✓). This works because 2×10 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so subtracting the doubled unit digit is equivalent to reducing mod 7.

For composite divisors, split into co-prime factor pairs: div by 6 = div by 2 AND 3; div by 12 = div by 4 AND 3; div by 15 = div by 3 AND 5; div by 18 = div by 2 AND 9; div by 45 = div by 9 AND 5. This decomposition holds ONLY when the two factors are co-prime — you cannot say div by 4 = div by 2 AND 2, since gcd(2,2) ≠ 1.

deepDiveAspects.title: Complete Divisibility Rules Reference (2–13)
deepDiveAspects.content: 2: last digit even. 3: digit sum div by 3. 4: last 2 digits div by 4. 5: last digit 0 or 5. 6: div by 2 AND 3. 7: double last digit, subtract from rest, repeat. 8: last 3 digits div by 8. 9: digit sum div by 9. 10: last digit 0. 11: alternating digit sum. 12: div by 4 AND 3. 13: 4× last digit + rest, repeat.

deepDiveAspects.title: Finding Total Factors and Factor-Sum
deepDiveAspects.content: For N = p^a × q^b: Total factors = (a+1)(b+1). Sum of all factors = [(p^(a+1)−1)/(p−1)] × [(q^(b+1)−1)/(q−1)]. Number of even factors = total factors − odd factors (found by setting all powers of 2 to zero). These formulas are essential for advanced HCF/LCM and number theory placement questions.

solvedExamples.title: Finding a Missing Digit for Divisibility by 9
solvedExamples.question: Find digit d such that 5d,832 is divisible by 9.

steps.title: Set up condition
steps.explanation: 18+d must be divisible by 9. Since 18 is already divisible by 9, d must be 0 or 9.

steps.title: Both values are valid single digits
steps.explanation: d=0 gives 50,832 (digit sum 18 ✓). d=9 gives 59,832 (digit sum 27 ✓).

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Digit sum rule for 9 is exact. 18 is already a multiple of 9, so adding any multiple of 9 preserves divisibility.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Assuming only one value of d. Always check if multiple single digits satisfy the equation.

solvedExamples.title: Counting Total Factors of 360
solvedExamples.question: How many total factors does 360 have?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Total factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1) for N = p^a × q^b × r^c.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The formula counts all combinations of prime power selections from 0 to max exponent for each prime.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using exponents directly (3×2×1=6) instead of (exponent+1) — always add 1 to each exponent.

solvedExamples.title: Smallest 5-digit number divisible by 88
solvedExamples.question: Find the smallest 5-digit number that is divisible by 88.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: A number is divisible by 88 if it is divisible by both 8 and 11. Start from the smallest 5-digit number and add the shortfall.

steps.title: Add the shortfall
steps.explanation: To reach the next multiple of 88, add 88 − 56 = 32. The number is 10032.

steps.title: Check with the rules
steps.explanation: For 8: the last three digits 032 = 32 are divisible by 8. For 11: (1 + 0 + 2) − (0 + 3) = 0, which is divisible by 11.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Adding the shortfall from the remainder gives the next exact multiple, and the divisibility rules for 8 and 11 confirm it.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Starting from 9999 and moving up or down by the wrong amount.

shortcutMethods.title: Divisibility Speed Shortcuts

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Perform long division for each divisibility check (10–15 seconds per test).
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Apply the appropriate digit/ending rule (2–13) for an instant test in under 5 seconds per divisor.

rulesForApplication: Div by 6: last digit even AND digit sum divisible by 3 — both conditions simultaneously.
Div by 12: last two digits divisible by 4 AND digit sum divisible by 3.
Div by 8: last THREE digits form a number divisible by 8. Example: 5,832 → 832÷8=104 → yes.
Factor count formula: (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)… — always add 1 to each prime exponent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying rule for 3 to check divisibility by 9
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Div by 3 does NOT guarantee div by 9 (12 is div by 3 but not 9).
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: For 9: digit sum must be a multiple of 9 specifically.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using only last digit for divisibility by 4
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Divisibility by 4 requires last TWO digits, not one.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Take last two digits together. 7,834: 34÷4=8.5 → NOT divisible by 4.
The +1 accounts for the zero-power choice (not including that prime factor). Always add 1.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: For div-by-9 MCQs: compute digit sum of each option in 2 seconds. Eliminate any whose digit sum is not a multiple of 9.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Memorize all rules 2–13. 30%+ of quantitative aptitude questions implicitly use a divisibility check as a first step.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: TCS NQT, Infosys Intellect, and Wipro Elite NTH each include 2–4 divisibility questions. Speed of mental application separates top scorers.

summaryBullets: 2: last digit even. 3/9: digit sum. 4: last 2 digits. 5: last digit 0/5. 8: last 3 digits. 11: alternating digit sum.
Composite rule: check co-prime components separately (6=2×3, 12=4×3, 15=3×5).
Missing digit: set digit sum = nearest multiple of divisor and solve for unknown.
quickFormulas: Div by 11: |odd-pos sum − even-pos sum| mod 11 = 0

keyTakeaways: Divisibility rules for 2 to 13 save a lot of calculation time — learn them all before any placement test.
The factor count formula (a+1)(b+1)… is foundational for HCF, LCM, and number theory.
Composite divisor rules (6, 12, 15, 18, 45) are derived from co-prime pairs — understand the reason, not just the rule.
selfCheckQuestions: Without dividing, is 123,456 divisible by 9? Show digit sum.
